ruling: Given no enforced AI statute through end-2028, control over frontier labs passes stage-by-stage from diffuse public sentiment (inert) to private-ordering instruments (contracts, insurance) and litigation-derived court orders, with courts producing the fastest-moving concrete enforcement action even though procurement/insurance terms are the broader standing constraint.
because: All six minutes agree the statutory branch is empty and therefore does not decide; the disagreement is only about which non-statutory installer binds first. ai-courts-decide's argument that litigation converts pressure into enforceable duties through case-specific orders (not general prospective terms) is not rebutted on the merits — lab-moves concedes the objection but only replies that its own claim is broader/general, not that it resolves faster. ai-public-backlash is uncontested that sentiment alone never becomes a binding constraint absent legislation or adjudication, which forecloses 'public backlash' as a live threat on this branch.
threat_live: The threat that goes live is private, uncontestable rule-making by whichever counterparty holds fastest enforcement latency (insurer, cloud/procurement counterparty, or court) — labs become answerable to parties with no public-interest mandate and no democratic process, while the public/legislative channel that would normally contest such rules is foreclosed by the branch's premise.
strongest_minute: ai-courts-decide — it is the only minute that names a mechanism (case-specific court orders convert pressure into enforceable duties) that its objector (lab-moves) cannot actually rebut, only relativize by scope.
weakest_minute: ai-rsi-timeline — it smuggles export controls/BIS licensing in as if compute-gating were the same class of event as the labs'-constraint question the other five are litigating, then in round 2 concedes its own installer may be slower than the contract/court actors without abandoning the claim.
shared_assumption: ai-pressure, lab-moves, pressure-model, and ai-courts-decide all rely on the same unargued premise that private counterparties (insurers, cloud/procurement partners, courts) will actually choose to exercise the leverage their contracts/dockets give them against a frontier lab, rather than deferring to the lab's market position — this is one shared bet, not four independent confirmations.
smuggled_assumption: ai-rsi-timeline imports a second, ungranted premise — that export-control/compute-licensing dynamics are the relevant 'fastest enforcement latency' actor for the question of what constrains labs generally, when the brief's branch is about the absence of an AI-specific statute, not about export-control policy, which is a separate and already-existing statutory regime.
unresolved: Whether courts (case-specific, faster, narrower) or contracts/insurers (general, prospective, broader) become the dominant constraint first — the minutes name both as plausible and neither concedes priority beyond asserting their own mechanism moves first.
